claims.text: The initial induction-melted Mg–Al–Cu–Zn–Gd alloy is in a non-equilibrium state.
The initial alloy contains a complex mixture of solid solutions and intermetallic compounds.
Annealing at 300–400 °C under controlled mildly oxidizing conditions triggers limited Mg diffusion and nanoscale segregation.
Segregated Mg oxidizes locally to form nanoscale MgO precipitates at phase boundaries.
The MgO precipitates form a passivating network that stabilizes the microstructure.
Phase-boundary MgO precipitates limit corrosion by acting as barriers to corrosive attack and reducing active corrosion sites.
Phase-boundary MgO precipitates encourage formation of a protective surface oxide scale at high temperature.
Mildly oxidizing annealing will produce a uniform dispersion of nanoscale MgO at phase boundaries.
Mildly oxidizing annealing will reduce corrosion current density relative to the as-cast and inert-annealed conditions.
Mildly oxidizing annealing will lower high-temperature oxidation mass gain relative to the as-cast and inert-annealed conditions.
The as-cast baseline lacks controlled Mg oxidation.
The as-cast baseline is expected to have higher corrosion rates than the mildly oxidizing annealed state.
The as-cast baseline is expected to have poorer high-temperature oxidation resistance than the mildly oxidizing annealed state.
The proposed hypothesis is bounded to induction-melted Mg–Al–Cu–Zn–Gd alloys with density below 6 g/cm³.
The proposed evolution may depend on annealing temperature, duration, and oxygen partial pressure.
Excessive or poorly controlled exposure may cause non-uniform oxidation or unexpected phase transformations.
Failure to increase nanoscale MgO relative to the inert-annealed control would falsify the proposed controlled-Mg-oxidation mechanism.
Failure to improve corrosion resistance or high-temperature oxidation behavior would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The baseline is inconsistently specified: some fields identify the as-cast alloy as the baseline, whereas the controlled experiment uses an inert- or reducing-atmosphere annealed sample as the control. The two-set falsification design does not explicitly include the as-cast comparator invoked in the predicted outcome.
